title: Mock test 1
summary: After this unit you have taken a complete IELTS Academic test under exam conditions and know your band in each paper.

items.title: Mock Listening test
body: Four parts, forty questions: about 23 minutes of recording, including time to read the questions, then two minutes to check your answers. Each recording plays once. You get time to read the questions before each part and again halfway through Parts 1 to 3, and half a minute to check at the end of Parts 1 to 3. Write as you listen and check spelling at the end. This is the real thing: no pausing.

items.title: Booking a kayaking trip
items.context: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a company to book a sea kayaking trip. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good morning, Coastline Kayak Tours, Anna speaking.
Hi there. I'd like to book one of your guided trips for next month, if you've got space.
Of course. Have you had a look at the trips on our website?
I have. We were thinking of the Island Trip, the one that goes round the lighthouse.
Ah, I should warn you that the Island Trip is for experienced paddlers only. It's about four hours on open water. Have any of your group kayaked before?
Not really. Just once on a lake.
In that case I'd recommend the Seal Bay trip. It stays inside the bay, so the water's much calmer, and you've got a very good chance of seeing seals on the rocks.
That sounds perfect, actually. Seal Bay, then.
Lovely. What date were you thinking of?
We arrive on the fifteenth of August, so any day after that. The sixteenth?
The sixteenth is fully booked, I'm afraid, and so is the seventeenth. The eighteenth has plenty of space.
The eighteenth's fine. We're there all week.
And how many people?
It was going to be four, but my brother can't come now, so it's three: two adults and my daughter.
Three. And how old is your daughter? The minimum age for Seal Bay is ten.
She's twelve. She'll be thirteen in September, but she's twelve at the moment.
That's fine. Can I have a name for the booking?
Daniel Pelham. That's P-E-L-H-A-M.
Thank you. And where are you staying while you're here? We like to know in case the weather changes and we need to contact you.
We've rented a cottage at Treloar Farm. That's T-R-E-L-O-A-R.
Oh, I know it. Just outside the village.
Before you hear the rest, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
Right, let me tell you about the arrangements on the day. Where we meet is important, because people often go to the wrong place.
Not the harbour café, then? That's where I assumed.
No. A lot of people go there, but we actually meet at the old lifeboat station, at the far end of the harbour. It's got a blue door, you can't miss it.
The old lifeboat station. And what time?

The trip starts at ten, but please arrive twenty minutes early so we can fit everyone with buoyancy aids and do the safety briefing. Our website says fifteen, but that's out of date. Twenty is what we ask now.
Twenty minutes, fine. Do we need to bring anything?

We provide wetsuits, buoyancy aids and waterproof jackets. You'll need a change of clothes for afterwards, and please wear old trainers. People think bare feet will be fine, but the rocks on the beach are very sharp.
Old trainers, got it. And the price?
It's forty-five pounds for each adult and thirty for under-sixteens. So for the three of you that comes to one hundred and twenty pounds.
That's fine. Can I pay by card now?
Yes. Oh, and one thing I should mention: if we have to cancel because of the weather, which does happen a few times each summer, you can either have a full refund or move to another day.
That's good to know. The forecast looked a bit mixed, actually.
We'll let you know by eight o'clock that morning at the latest. So, shall I take your card details?
Yes, please.
Lovely. I'll take the details and email you a confirmation.

items.title: The new Central Library
items.context: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a public library talking to visitors about its renovation. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the newly reopened Central Library. My name's Helen Grant and I'm the library manager. After eighteen months of building work, I'm delighted to show you what we've done. I'll start with a quick guide to the ground floor, and then tell you about some of our new services.

We're standing just inside the main entrance. Immediately to your right is something many of you asked for in our consultation: a café. It has windows onto the square, and you're welcome to take library books in there, though we do ask you to be careful with the coffee.

Regular visitors will remember that the children's library used to be just here on the left, by the entrance. That space now holds the self-service machines for borrowing and returning books. The children's library has moved to the far left-hand corner of the building, as far from the street as possible. It's quieter there, and parents told us they felt it was safer away from the doors.

In the middle of the floor, under the glass roof, you'll see our new computer area, with forty computers available free of charge, plus printers and a scanner. Straight ahead, in the middle of the far wall, is the local history room. That holds our collection of maps, old newspapers and photographs of the town, and staff there can help you trace your family history.

And if you need somewhere silent to work, the quiet study area is in the far right-hand corner. We've put it there because it's well away from the café and the entrance, and the walls have been specially insulated against noise. The newspapers and magazines are halfway along the left-hand wall, and the toilets and lifts are halfway along the wall on the right.
Before you hear the rest, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

Now let me tell you about what's new beyond the building itself. We've introduced a number of services this year. Perhaps the most popular so far has been our tool library. For a small annual fee, members can borrow things like drills, ladders and gardening equipment, just as they would borrow a book. The other service I'd particularly like to mention is our home delivery scheme. Volunteers bring books to people who can't easily get to the library, because of illness or disability, for example. We had hoped to start a film club as well, but that's had to be postponed until next year, and the evening language classes we used to run are, sadly, no longer possible because of staffing.

Some of you have asked about opening hours. We now open on Sundays, from eleven until four, which we haven't done for many years. To make that possible, we close an hour earlier on Saturdays than we used to. Weekday hours are unchanged.

The renovation cost just over four million pounds. Most of the money came from a national heritage fund, because the building is over a hundred years old. The council contributed about a quarter of the cost, and a local fundraising campaign paid for the furniture in the children's library.

One thing I'm particularly proud of is how much of the original building we've kept. The architects were asked to preserve the Victorian reading room ceiling, and you can see that it's been beautifully restored. What's entirely new is the roof garden, which will open to the public in the spring once the plants have had time to establish themselves.

Finally, we're keen to hear what you think. There are feedback cards on every desk, but the easiest way to get in touch is through the short survey on our website. We read every response. Thank you, and enjoy exploring.

items.why: "Most of the money came from a national heritage fund"; the council paid about a quarter.

items.title: A car-free town centre
items.context: Part 3. You will hear two students, Ella and Kofi, discussing a case study with their tutor, Dr Shaw. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: So, you're doing your case study on Marlbury and its car-free centre. Why Marlbury, out of all the towns that have tried this?
We looked at a few. Some of the big cities have done it, but they've got underground systems and huge bus networks, so it's hard to apply the lessons anywhere else.

Marlbury's a typical market town, about forty thousand people, and it banned cars from the centre eight years ago. So there's enough time to see the long-term effects, and the results are relevant to lots of other towns.
Good reasoning. What was the main aim of the scheme when it was introduced? I've seen different accounts.

So have we. The newspapers at the time made it all about pollution, but when you read the council's original documents, the main concern was road safety. There'd been a series of accidents involving pedestrians on the high street.
Air quality was mentioned, but it was definitely secondary.
Interesting. That's worth making a point of. And how did local businesses react?
Badly at first. There was a petition with over two thousand signatures, mostly from shopkeepers who thought they'd lose customers who drove in.

But by about the third year, most of them had changed their minds. Footfall went up, and the empty shops started filling. The traders' association actually campaigned against reopening the street when the council considered it.
What about the people who found it hardest, elderly residents, disabled people?

That's the weakest part of the scheme, in our view. They introduced a shuttle bus, but it only runs every half an hour and not at all on Sundays. Several people we spoke to said they'd stopped going into town.
Has the council done anything in response?
They're reviewing the shuttle timetable this year, apparently, and there's been talk of electric buggies for people with mobility problems. But nothing's actually been decided.
Then you should make that point carefully: promised improvements aren't the same as results.
Before you hear the rest, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
Now, what do you see as the main reasons the scheme succeeded overall?
We think two things made the difference. First, the council spent a lot on the streets themselves: new paving, trees, benches. It became somewhere people wanted to be.
And second, they built a large car park on the edge of the centre, just five minutes' walk away. People could still drive into town; they just couldn't drive through it.
Some people say the market was the key, because they moved it into the high street, but it was already doing well before the change.
And the cycle lanes were nice, but cycling's still only a tiny share of journeys.
Fine. Now let's talk about your sources. You've used several kinds of data. How reliable are they?
The council's traffic counts are the most useful. They go back fifteen years, so we can compare before and after.
And the business survey by the chamber of commerce?
We're a bit wary of that. The chamber campaigned for the scheme, so they had an interest in showing it worked. The questions are quite leading.
Fair. What about the air quality figures?
They're good data, but there's only one monitoring station, and it was moved halfway through the period. So the readings before and after aren't really comparable.
And your own interviews?
Really interesting, but we only managed eleven, so we can't generalise from them. We'll use them for quotations to illustrate points.
Good. Make sure each of those judgements is in the methodology section. Anything else?
Just the national census figures on car ownership. They're reliable, but they're from three years ago.
That's fine as long as you say so.
Will do. We're aiming to send you a draft of the findings chapter by the end of next month.
Good. Concentrate on the evidence, and keep the recommendations short. I look forward to reading it.

sets.instr: Questions 21-24. Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: Why did the students choose Marlbury for their case study?
options: A  It was the first town to ban cars.
B  It has an excellent public transport system.
C  Its experience is relevant to many other towns.
items.why: "The results are relevant to lots of other towns"; big cities with large transport systems were rejected as hard to apply elsewhere.

items.q: According to the council's documents, the main aim of the scheme was to
items.why: Newspapers stressed pollution, "but… the main concern was road safety".

items.q: How did most local shopkeepers feel after three years?
options: B  They still opposed the scheme.
C  They wanted cars allowed at weekends.
items.why: "Most of them had changed their minds"; the traders' association campaigned against reopening the street.

items.q: What do the students see as the main weakness of the scheme?
options: A  The cost of the new paving.
B  The location of the car park.
C  Poor provision for people with limited mobility.
items.why: "That's the weakest part of the scheme": the shuttle bus is infrequent, and elderly and disabled people stopped going into town.

items.q: Which TWO factors do the students think made the scheme successful?
options: E  a car park close to the centre
items.why: "Two things made the difference": new paving, trees and benches (A), and "a large car park on the edge of the centre" (E). The market was already doing well before the change, cycling is still "a tiny share" of journeys, and the shuttle bus is the scheme's weakness.

sets.instr: Questions 27-30. What do the students say about each source? Choose the correct letter, A-F.

options: B  It is the most useful source.
C  It is based on too few people.
D  Changes in method make comparison difficult.
F  It was difficult to obtain.
items.why: Business survey: the chamber "had an interest in showing it worked". Air quality: the station "was moved halfway through". Interviews: "only… eleven". Census: "from three years ago". B describes the traffic counts, which are not asked about.

items.title: How migrating birds find their way
items.context: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture on animal behaviour. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Today I want to look at one of the great puzzles of animal behaviour: how migrating birds find their way. Every year, billions of birds travel thousands of kilometres between their breeding and wintering grounds, and many return to exactly the same nest site, sometimes to the same tree. Some, like many songbirds, make the journey alone and at night. So how do they do it? The short answer is that birds use not one system but several, and they seem to be able to switch between them depending on the conditions.

Let's start with the sun. In the nineteen-fifties, researchers showed that caged starlings, which became restless at migration time, oriented themselves in a particular direction when they could see the sun. When the apparent position of the sun was shifted using mirrors, the birds changed direction accordingly. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so to use it as a compass a bird must also know what time it is. In other words, the sun compass depends on the bird's internal clock. If you shift a bird's clock by keeping it under artificial light for several days, it makes predictable errors in direction.

Many species migrate at night, however, and for them the stars are important. Some of the most elegant experiments in this field were carried out in a planetarium, where researchers could control what the birds saw. They found that young birds of one North American species did not inherit a map of particular constellations. Instead, they learned to identify the point around which the night sky appears to rotate, which in the northern hemisphere is close to the Pole Star. Birds raised under an artificial sky that rotated around a different star simply treated that star as north.

The third system is the one that most fascinates researchers: the magnetic sense. Experiments with European robins in the nineteen-sixties showed that birds kept in a cage with no view of the sky could still orient themselves correctly, and that altering the magnetic field around the cage changed the direction they chose. Interestingly, the robins' compass does not work like ours. It doesn't distinguish north from south by polarity. Instead, it seems to detect the angle at which the field lines meet the Earth's surface, which tells the bird whether it is heading towards the pole or towards the equator. Exactly how birds sense the field is still debated. One leading theory involves chemical reactions in the eye, which would mean that birds may, in some sense, see the magnetic field.

Then there is smell. For a long time, birds were thought to have a poor sense of smell, but we now know that this isn't true. Homing pigeons whose sense of smell has been blocked are much less successful at finding their way home from unfamiliar places, and some seabirds appear to use odours carried on the wind to locate feeding areas and their nesting colonies across vast stretches of open ocean.

Finally, there are landmarks. Close to the end of a journey, birds certainly use familiar features such as coastlines, rivers and mountain ranges, and many migratory routes follow them. Some researchers have also suggested that birds may detect very low-frequency sound, generated by waves or wind over mountains, though the evidence for this is still limited.

A key question is how much of this is learned and how much is inherited. A famous experiment in the Netherlands in the nineteen-fifties gives us a clue. Thousands of starlings were caught during their autumn migration and transported several hundred kilometres to the south before being released. The adult birds corrected their course and reached their usual wintering grounds. The young birds, making their first migration, did not. They continued to fly in the same direction as before and ended up in an entirely different region. This suggests that first-time migrants rely on an inherited programme, something like 'fly south-west for so many weeks', while experienced birds have developed a true map that allows them to work out where they are.

This has important implications for conservation. If young birds follow a fixed programme, they may be poorly equipped to cope when the places they rely on change, for example when stopover sites where they rest and feed are lost to development. And artificial light at night is known to disorientate migrating birds, particularly in bad weather, when they may be drawn towards illuminated buildings. Some cities now turn off unnecessary lighting in tall buildings during peak migration periods, a simple measure that appears to save large numbers of birds. In the next lecture we'll look at how tracking technology is transforming what we know about these journeys.

items.title: Mock Reading test
body: Three passages, forty questions, sixty minutes, with no extra time to transfer answers. Passages get harder as you go: aim for about 17, 20 and 23 minutes. Never leave a blank.

paragraphs.text: Few objects are as familiar, or as little considered, as the pencil. It is cheap, reliable and almost infinitely forgiving: a mark can be made, rubbed out and made again. Yet its history involves a remarkable geological accident, a century of smuggling and guarded mines, and an ingenious solution devised under the pressure of war. It also involves a persistent misunderstanding, because the material at the heart of every pencil has never been lead.

The story begins in the sixteenth century in Borrowdale, a valley in what is now the county of Cumbria in north-west England. There, a deposit of unusually pure graphite was discovered. According to local tradition, shepherds were the first to make use of it, marking their sheep with lumps of the soft, black substance. Graphite is a form of carbon, but at the time nobody knew that. Because it left a grey mark similar to that made by lead, which had been used for writing and ruling lines since Roman times, it was taken to be a kind of lead and was known as 'black lead' or 'plumbago'. The name 'graphite', from a Greek word meaning 'to write', was not introduced until the late eighteenth century, by which time the misunderstanding had become fixed in everyday language.

Borrowdale graphite proved valuable for more than writing. It could withstand very high temperatures, and it was used to line the moulds in which cannonballs were cast, giving them a smoother finish. Its military importance, combined with the fact that no comparable deposit had been found anywhere else, made it a strategic resource. The mine was opened only for limited periods so that the market would not be flooded, and guards were posted to prevent theft. Even so, workers smuggled graphite out, and a flourishing black market developed. In the eighteenth century an Act of Parliament made stealing it a serious criminal offence.

The first pencils were simply sticks of graphite, sawn from the solid mineral and wrapped in string or sheepskin to keep the user's fingers clean. Craftsmen later began to insert the sticks into hollowed-out pieces of wood, and the familiar wooden pencil was born. For two centuries, the best pencils in Europe depended on Borrowdale graphite, because the graphite found elsewhere was too impure and crumbly to be cut into sticks.

This dependence became a serious problem for France in the 1790s, when war with Britain cut off its supply. The French government asked Nicolas-Jacques Conté, a scientist and inventor, to find an alternative. His solution, patented in 1795, was to grind impure graphite into a powder, mix it with clay and water, form the mixture into thin rods and fire them in a kiln. The method had an unexpected advantage. By varying the proportion of clay, Conté could make the pencil harder or softer: more clay produced a harder pencil with a lighter line, more graphite a softer one with a darker line. The process is still the basis of pencil manufacture today, and it freed pencil-making from its reliance on a single English valley.

Other refinements followed. Manufacturers developed systems for grading hardness, the most widespread of which uses the letter H for hard and B for black, with HB in the middle. Woods were chosen for their ability to be sharpened cleanly; cedar became the preferred material because it is soft, straight-grained and does not splinter easily. Many pencils were given a six-sided shape, which is more comfortable to hold for some users and, just as importantly, stops the pencil rolling off a sloping desk.

The eraser has its own history. In 1770 the English scientist Joseph Priestley noted that a substance from South America, which he called 'rubber' for exactly this reason, was excellent at removing pencil marks. Before that, people had used pieces of bread. Attaching an eraser to the end of the pencil itself came considerably later, and the practice has never been universal: many pencils sold in Europe still have no eraser at all.

Today, billions of pencils are made every year, and despite repeated predictions of its decline, and although it is no longer the everyday writing tool it once was, the pencil has survived the arrival of the typewriter, the ballpoint pen and the computer. Its advantages are hard to beat. Carpenters, artists and engineers continue to favour it for particular tasks. It works at any angle and in any temperature, it does not leak or dry out, and its marks are permanent enough to last for centuries yet easy to remove when a mistake is made. The graphite deposit at Borrowdale, meanwhile, has long since been exhausted.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every animal that scientists have studied closely appears to sleep, or to enter a state that closely resembles sleep. Mammals and birds do it, as do reptiles, fish and insects; fruit flies, which have been used extensively in sleep research, show periods of inactivity during which they are harder to rouse, and if they are deprived of this rest they compensate by resting more afterwards. The universality of sleep is puzzling, because a sleeping animal is vulnerable. It cannot feed, mate or watch for predators. Whatever sleep provides must be valuable enough to outweigh these risks.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most striking evidence that sleep is fundamental comes from an animal without a brain. In a study published in 2017, researchers examined a species of upside-down jellyfish, which spends most of its time lying on the sea floor, pulsing rhythmically. At night, the pulsing slowed, the jellyfish responded more slowly to stimulation, and when kept awake by pulses of water, it was less active the following day. These are the standard behavioural criteria for sleep. If a creature with only a simple network of nerves sleeps, then sleep may have arisen very early in the history of animal life, long before brains evolved.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some animals have found ingenious ways to reconcile the need for sleep with the demands of their environment. Dolphins, which must surface regularly to breathe, sleep with one half of the brain at a time. While one hemisphere shows the slow electrical waves characteristic of deep sleep, the other remains awake, and the eye connected to the waking half often stays open. After a period the two halves swap roles. This arrangement, known as unihemispheric sleep, allows the animal to keep swimming, to breathe and to remain alert to danger. Several species of bird can do something similar. Fur seals, which divide their time between land and sea, show a particularly flexible pattern: on land they sleep much like other mammals, but in the water they switch largely to sleeping with one hemisphere at a time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Birds that fly for long periods raise an obvious question: can they sleep in the air? For frigatebirds, which can stay aloft over the ocean for weeks at a time, the answer appears to be yes. Researchers who fitted the birds with small devices to record their brain activity found that they did sleep during flight, sometimes with one hemisphere and sometimes with both, but only in bursts lasting a few seconds and for a total of less than an hour a day. On land, the same birds slept for more than twelve hours a day. Flight, it seems, allows sleep but not much of it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The amount of sleep animals need varies enormously, and the reasons are not fully understood. Giraffes, which are large and vulnerable to predators when lying down, sleep relatively little, often in short periods totalling a few hours a day. Some bats, by contrast, are estimated to sleep for around twenty hours a day. One proposed explanation links sleep to diet: animals whose food is low in energy, such as grass, need to spend many hours eating, leaving less time for sleep. Another emphasises the risk of predation. Neither explanation accounts for all the variation, and it is likely that several factors are involved. Domestic and captive animals add a further complication, since their sleep is shaped by human routines and the absence of predators as well as by biology.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The function of sleep remains one of the central questions of biology. One long-standing theory holds that sleep conserves energy, since metabolism slows during rest. Another emphasises the brain: during sleep, recently acquired memories appear to be strengthened and reorganised, and people who sleep after learning generally remember more. A more recent proposal, based on experiments with mice published in 2013, suggests that sleep allows the brain to clear away waste products that accumulate during waking hours, because the flow of fluid through brain tissue increases markedly during sleep. These theories are not mutually exclusive, and sleep may well serve several purposes at once.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is clear is that sleep cannot simply be dispensed with. Animals deprived of it show impaired performance and, if deprivation continues, serious harm to health. In humans, even modest but persistent shortfalls are associated with an increased risk of accidents, weakened immunity and a range of long-term health problems. The jellyfish and the frigatebird, in their different ways, suggest that evolution has found it easier to work around the need for sleep than to eliminate it.

sets.instr: Questions 14-17. The passage has seven paragraphs, A-G. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.

rows.label: a reference to the dangers that sleeping animals face
a suggestion that sleep may have evolved before brains
a possible link between what an animal eats and how long it sleeps
a mention of the effects of insufficient sleep on human health

items.why: A: a sleeping animal "is vulnerable" and cannot watch for predators. B: sleep "may have arisen… long before brains evolved". E: "One proposed explanation links sleep to diet." G: shortfalls in humans are linked to accidents and weakened immunity.

sets.instr: Questions 18-21. Match each statement with the correct animal, A-E.

rows.label: show sleep-like behaviour despite having no brain
often keep one eye open while sleeping
sleep much less when travelling than when on land
may spend most of the day asleep

items.why: Jellyfish (paragraph B) = D: they sleep with "only a simple network of nerves" and no brain. Dolphins (paragraph C) = A: "the eye connected to the waking half often stays open". Frigatebirds (paragraph D) = B: under an hour a day in flight, more than twelve hours on land. Bats (paragraph E) = E: "around twenty hours a day".

sets.instr: Questions 22-26. Complete the summary below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

items.text: Fruit flies deprived of rest make up for it by ___ afterwards.
items.why: Paragraph A: "they compensate by resting more afterwards".

items.text: Dolphins need to stay partly awake because they must regularly ___ to breathe.
items.why: Paragraph C: dolphins "must surface regularly to breathe".

items.text: Their sleep pattern is called ___.
items.why: Paragraph C: "known as unihemispheric sleep". *Unihemispheric* alone is also accepted, since *sleep* is understood.

items.text: One theory states that sleep conserves energy because ___ slows down.
items.why: Paragraph F: "metabolism slows during rest".

items.text: A 2013 study suggests that during sleep the brain clears away ___.
items.why: Paragraph F: sleep "allows the brain to clear away waste products"; *waste* alone is also accepted.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every translator knows the experience: a sentence that is perfectly clear in the original refuses to come across intact. The difficulty is rarely a missing word. Dictionaries will usually supply something. It is that the word supplied carries a different set of associations, belongs to a different register, or sits within a different web of grammatical expectations. The popular image of translation as the substitution of equivalent words, as though languages were codes for a shared set of meanings, survives largely because most people never have to do it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Linguists have long recognised that languages divide up experience in different ways. Some distinguish between kinds of snow or rice that others lump together; some oblige their speakers to mark whether information was witnessed directly or heard from others; some have no grammatical tense at all and rely on context to locate events in time. It does not follow, as some enthusiasts have claimed, that speakers of different languages inhabit incommensurable mental worlds. People routinely express ideas for which their language has no single word, and children acquire whatever distinctions their language requires without apparent difficulty. But it does follow that a translation cannot be judged simply by whether each element of the original has a counterpart in the result.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The notion of equivalence has accordingly been refined. Translation theorists distinguish between formal equivalence, which keeps as close as possible to the structure and wording of the source, and dynamic or functional equivalence, which aims to produce in the new reader the effect the original produced in its first readers. The distinction is useful, though it is sometimes presented as a choice between fidelity and freedom, a framing that seems to me unhelpful. A translation that follows the original word for word may be faithful to its surface while betraying its tone; one that departs from the wording may be the more faithful to what the author was trying to do.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Literary translation makes these tensions especially visible. A poem's meaning is inseparable from its sound, its rhythm and the associations of individual words, none of which survive transfer into another language unchanged. Translators of verse must decide which features to preserve and which to sacrifice: rhyme or sense, metre or idiom, the strangeness of the original or the naturalness of the result. There is no correct answer, which is why great poems are retranslated in every generation. Each version reveals something that others have missed, and none is final.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It might be supposed that technical and commercial texts escape these difficulties, and to a degree they do. A safety instruction or a contract clause has a purpose that can be specified, and success can be measured by whether the purpose is achieved. Yet even here, equivalence is less straightforward than it appears. Legal concepts are embedded in particular systems of law, and a term that seems to have an obvious counterpart may carry quite different obligations. Marketing material must be adapted, sometimes radically, to a new culture's sense of humour, politeness or taste. The translator of such texts is often doing something closer to rewriting than to transfer.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The rise of machine translation has given these old debates new urgency. Modern systems, trained on vast quantities of existing translations, produce fluent and often accurate results, and for many purposes they are entirely adequate. It would be foolish to pretend otherwise. What they do less reliably is make the kinds of judgement described above: recognising irony, choosing between registers, noticing when a literal rendering is technically correct but culturally tone-deaf. Their very fluency can be misleading, since a smooth sentence invites trust in a way that a clumsy one does not, and errors of meaning are harder to spot when the surface is polished.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the human translator is irreplaceable in every context; for routine texts the economics are already decisive. But it does suggest that we should be wary of the assumption, encouraged by the success of automated systems, that translation is fundamentally a matter of finding equivalents. If anything, the limits of machine translation have clarified what the human translator contributes: not a better dictionary, but an interpretation. Every translation is a reading of the original, shaped by the translator's understanding of its purpose and its audience, and the best translations are those that make their interpretive choices with full awareness that they are choices.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: This is not a counsel of despair. That perfect equivalence is unattainable does not mean that translation fails; it means that its success must be measured differently. A translation should be judged not by whether it reproduces the original, which no translation can, but by whether it gives its readers a faithful and illuminating access to it. On that measure, translation is one of the most remarkable things that language allows us to do, precisely because it is not mechanical.

sets.instr: Questions 27-32. Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer? Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

items.statement: The common view of translation persists because few people have direct experience of translating.
items.why: Paragraph A: the popular image "survives largely because most people never have to do it".

items.statement: Differences between languages mean that their speakers cannot understand each other's ideas.
items.why: Paragraph B: "It does not follow… that speakers of different languages inhabit incommensurable mental worlds."

items.statement: Presenting translation as a choice between fidelity and freedom is helpful.
items.why: Paragraph C: "a framing that seems to me unhelpful".

items.statement: Older translations of poems are generally better than recent ones.
items.why: Paragraph D says each version reveals something and none is final, but makes no comparison between older and newer translations.

items.statement: Machine translation is sufficient for many purposes.
items.why: Paragraph F: "for many purposes they are entirely adequate. It would be foolish to pretend otherwise."

items.statement: Human translators will remain necessary for all types of text.
items.why: Paragraph G: "None of this means that the human translator is irreplaceable in every context; for routine texts the economics are already decisive."

sets.instr: Questions 33-36. Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: In paragraph B, the examples of snow, rice and tense are used to show that
options: A  some languages are more precise than others.
B  translation between some languages is impossible.
D  children find some languages hard to learn.
items.why: "Languages divide up experience in different ways" is the claim the examples illustrate. The writer explicitly rejects the stronger conclusion in B.

items.q: What does the writer suggest about a word-for-word translation?
options: A  It may misrepresent the tone of the original.
B  It is always the most faithful.
C  It is suitable only for poetry.
D  It is the aim of functional equivalence.
items.why: Paragraph C: it "may be faithful to its surface while betraying its tone".

items.q: According to paragraph E, translating marketing material
options: A  is easier than translating contracts.
B  should be done by machines.
items.why: Marketing material "must be adapted, sometimes radically"; the translator is doing "something closer to rewriting".

items.q: Why does the writer consider the fluency of machine translation a potential problem?
options: A  It makes the output too informal.
B  It is achieved by copying human translations.
C  It may hide errors by encouraging trust.
items.why: Paragraph F: "a smooth sentence invites trust… and errors of meaning are harder to spot when the surface is polished".

sets.instr: Questions 37-40. Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-G.

items.q: Choose the correct ending, A-G, for each sentence.
options: A  is shaped by an interpretation of the original.
B  has a purpose that can be clearly defined.
C  should reproduce every element of the source.
D  depends on sound and rhythm as well as meaning.
E  is a reason to abandon translation.
F  should be judged by the access it gives readers to the original.
items.why: The meaning of a poem = D: it "is inseparable from its sound, its rhythm" (paragraph D). A safety instruction = B: it "has a purpose that can be specified" (paragraph E). Every translation = A: it "is a reading of the original" (paragraph G). A successful translation = F: it is judged "by whether it gives its readers a faithful and illuminating access to it" (paragraph H).

items.title: Mock Writing test
body: Two tasks in sixty minutes. Spend about 20 minutes on Task 1 and 40 on Task 2, which counts twice as much. Plan before you write, and leave two or three minutes to check.

items.prompt:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The bar chart below shows the average number of hours per week that people in three age groups in the town of Calderford spent on four leisure activities in 2024.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

visual.title: Average hours per week spent on four leisure activities, by age group, Calderford, 2024

plan: Paraphrase: what the chart measures, where, when, the four activities and the three age groups.
Overview: which activity takes the most hours in each age group, and which group spends least time on the four combined.
Body 1: the two screen activities, which move in opposite directions as age rises.
Body 2: sport and reading, then the combined totals.

text: The bar chart compares the average weekly hours that people in three age groups in Calderford spent on four leisure activities in 2024.

Overall, screen-based activities accounted for most of the hours spent on these four pastimes in every age group, but the type of screen changed with age: social media led among the youngest, and television, by a wide margin, among the oldest. The middle group spent the least time on all four combined.

The two screen activities moved in opposite directions. Young adults aged 16 to 29 spent 14 hours a week on social media, compared with 8 hours watching television and films. Among those aged 30 to 49 the position was reversed, with 10.5 hours of viewing against 7 hours online, and in the oldest group the gap widened dramatically: viewing rose to 17 hours, while social media use fell to just 2.5.

Sport and exercise peaked among 16- to 29-year-olds (6 hours), dipped to 3.5 in middle age and rose again to 5 among the over-50s. Reading, by contrast, rose with age, slightly at first (from 2 to 3 hours) and then sharply to 7.5 in the oldest group, more than three times as much as the youngest. In total, the four activities filled 24 hours a week for the middle group, against 30 and 32 for the younger and older groups.
notes: The overview picks out the two patterns that matter most, the shift from social media to television with age and the lower total for the middle group, without a single figure.
Each body paragraph groups related activities: first the two screen activities, which move in opposite directions, then the two smaller ones.
Figures are selected and compared rather than listed: the end points, the reversal in the middle group and a multiple (*more than three times as much*: 7.5 against 2 hours).
Every number matches the chart, including the totals (30, 24 and 32 hours), which the writer has added up rather than estimated.
Comparative language is varied and precise: *the position was reversed*, *the gap widened dramatically*, *dipped*, *rose again*, *by contrast*.
The age groups are named in several ways (*young adults aged 16 to 29*, *the over-50s*, *the oldest group*), which avoids repetition without losing accuracy.

items.prompt:
You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

Write about the following topic:

In many countries, museums and art galleries are now free for everyone to enter.

Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
plan: Paragraph 3: the main advantage (access for those who would be excluded).
Paragraph 4: further advantages (public ownership; wider economic benefit).

text: In a number of countries, national museums and galleries have abolished admission charges, so that anyone can walk in off the street and spend an afternoon among paintings, fossils or ancient manuscripts without paying. While this policy has real costs, I believe its advantages are considerably greater.

The disadvantages are essentially financial. Museums are expensive to run, and every pound not collected at the door must be found elsewhere, whether from taxation, private sponsors or the sale of coffee and souvenirs. In practice, free entry may leave institutions more exposed to cuts in public funding, and some argue that it is unfair for taxpayers who never visit to subsidise those who do, particularly tourists. There is also a risk that popular museums become overcrowded, which can detract from the experience of every visitor.

However, these problems are manageable, whereas the benefits of free access go to the heart of what museums are for. Charges, even modest ones, discourage precisely the people who stand to gain most: families on low incomes, students, and those who have never felt that such places were meant for them. When entry is free, a museum ceases to be a planned and paid-for outing and becomes somewhere one can drop into for twenty minutes to see a single painting. Such casual, repeated visits are arguably how a lasting interest in art or history is formed.

Moreover, the collections in national museums are, in a meaningful sense, already owned by the public, often acquired with public money or donated for the nation's benefit. Charging people to see what is theirs sits uneasily with that principle. Free entry can also bring wider economic gains, since visitors who pay nothing at the door often spend money in cafés, shops and surrounding businesses.
On balance, then, while free admission places a genuine burden on public finances, this is a price worth paying for institutions that are open to everyone, not only to those who can afford a ticket.
notes: The question asks whether advantages outweigh disadvantages, and the essay answers it directly in the introduction and conclusion, with a clear, consistent position.
The disadvantages are presented fairly and specifically (funding exposure, fairness to non-visitors, overcrowding) before being weighed, which makes the judgement convincing.
Each body paragraph is built around one controlling idea and developed with explanation rather than lists of points.
Cohesion is achieved through reference and logical framing ('However, these problems are manageable, whereas…', 'Such casual, repeated visits') rather than mechanical linkers.
Precise collocation and natural register: 'go to the heart of', 'sits uneasily with', 'drop into', 'detract from the experience', 'a price worth paying'.
A wide range of complex structures, including relative and participle clauses, nominalisation and concessive structures, used without error.

items.title: Mock Speaking test
body: Answer each question aloud as if the examiner were in front of you, recording yourself if you can, then compare your answers with the models.

Part 1 lasts four to five minutes: after checking your identity, the examiner asks about your work or studies and then two other familiar topics, and each answer takes about 20-30 seconds. In Part 2 you have one minute to prepare and up to two minutes to speak, followed by one or two short questions. Part 3 answers take around 40-50 seconds each.

questions: Do you work or are you a student?
What does a typical working day involve for you?
What do you find most challenging about your job?
Is it a job you would recommend to young people?

text: I work. I'm a pharmacist at a large hospital, so I spend most of my time checking prescriptions and advising doctors and nurses on medicines. It's not the most glamorous job in the world, but it's rarely boring.

It varies quite a lot, actually. Mornings are usually spent on the wards, going through patients' medication with the medical team. The afternoons are more about problem-solving: chasing up a missing dose, say, or working out which drugs are safe to combine for someone who's taking eight different things.

Probably the pace, combined with the stakes. On a busy day you're making a lot of decisions very quickly, and there's no room for a careless mistake, because a wrong dose can do real harm. Staying sharp at the end of a long shift is harder than people imagine.

I would, yes, as long as they're genuinely interested in people as well as science. A lot of students choose pharmacy because they're good at chemistry, and then discover that half the job is explaining things to anxious patients. If you enjoy both sides, it's hugely rewarding.
notes: Each answer gives a direct response in the first few words, then one or two extensions: a detail, an example or a condition.
The job is explained in everyday terms (*checking prescriptions*, *chasing up a missing dose*, *safe to combine*) rather than in technical jargon that tells the examiner nothing about your range.
Natural spoken features (*actually*, *say*, *as long as*) and an honest qualification (*not the most glamorous job in the world*) make the answers sound spontaneous rather than prepared.
Grammar follows the meaning: present simple for routine, a passive for what usually happens (*Mornings are usually spent*), and a real conditional for advice (*If you enjoy both sides, it's...*).

phrases: It's not the most glamorous job in the world, but…
It varies quite a lot, actually
there's no room for a careless mistake
as long as they're genuinely interested in…

questions: Can you describe the neighbourhood where you live?
What do you like most about living there?
How has your neighbourhood changed in recent years?
Would you like to live there in the future?

text: Oh, it's a fairly quiet residential area on the edge of the city centre. Mostly terraced houses, a couple of parks, and a high street with the usual mix of cafés and small shops. It's not exactly glamorous, but it's got a nice, settled feel to it.

I'd say the best thing is that you can do almost everything on foot. I can walk to the station in ten minutes, and there's a fantastic bakery round the corner, which is probably a bit dangerous for me, to be honest.

Not much, actually. A few years ago the old cinema was turned into flats, which people were quite upset about, and a lot of the independent shops have been replaced by chains. But on the whole it's stayed pretty much the same.
In the long run, probably not. It's ideal for where I am in life at the moment, but if I had a family I think I'd want a bit more space and a garden, so I might look further out.
notes: Each answer is direct, then extended with a reason or example, which is exactly the right length for Part 1 (around 20-30 seconds).
Natural spoken features: 'Oh,', 'to be honest', 'not exactly glamorous', 'pretty much the same', 'In the long run'.
Precise vocabulary for the topic without sounding rehearsed: 'terraced houses', 'residential area', 'replaced by chains', 'a settled feel'.
A range of grammar used naturally: present perfect for change, a second conditional ('if I had a family, I'd want…'), passives ('was turned into flats').

questions: How often do you listen to music?
What kind of music do you enjoy?
Did you learn to play an instrument when you were younger?
Do you think children should learn to play a musical instrument?

text: Pretty much every day, yes, usually on my commute or when I'm cooking. I find it really helps me switch off at the end of the day.
It depends on my mood, really. I listen to a lot of jazz, but I've also got a bit of a soft spot for eighties pop, which my friends never let me forget.
I had piano lessons for a few years as a child, but I gave up when I was about twelve, which I now slightly regret. I can still pick out a tune, but that's about it.

I think so, yes. Music's one of those things that's genuinely good for children: it teaches discipline and concentration, and it's something they can enjoy for the rest of their lives, even if they never become very good at it.
notes: Answers are concise but never minimal: each adds a personal detail that makes the response sound authentic.
Idiomatic but unforced language: 'switch off', 'a soft spot for', 'never let me forget', 'pick out a tune'.
The final answer moves smoothly from personal to general, which is good practice for Part 3.

items.topic: A skill learnt as an adult

cue.task: Describe a skill you learnt as an adult.
cue.close: and explain why learning this skill was important to you.

followups: Is there another skill you would like to learn as an adult?

text: I'd like to talk about learning to swim properly, which is something I only did in my late twenties. I could sort of keep myself afloat as a child, but I'd never really learnt, and I was quite embarrassed about it.

What happened was that a friend invited me on a holiday that involved quite a lot of sea swimming, and I realised I'd either have to admit I couldn't swim or do something about it. So I signed up for an adult beginners' course at my local pool. It was one evening a week for about ten weeks, with a really patient instructor and about six other people, all of us in roughly the same boat, so to speak. On the first evening we all stood in the shallow end looking at each other nervously, and I remember thinking that at least nobody I knew could see me.

The hardest part, honestly, wasn't the technique. It was the breathing. I had this deep-seated panic about putting my face in the water, and for the first few weeks I just couldn't relax. The instructor had us doing these very simple exercises, just blowing bubbles, really, until it stopped feeling threatening. And then quite suddenly, around week five, something clicked, and I managed a whole length of front crawl without stopping.

I think the reason it meant so much to me is that it was the first time in years I'd been a complete beginner at something. As an adult you get used to being reasonably competent, and it was humbling, but also oddly liberating, to be really bad at something and gradually improve. It's also made me much more sympathetic to people who take up something late, because I know how much courage it takes just to turn up. And the holiday was wonderful, by the way. I spent most of it in the sea.
notes: The talk covers every bullet point naturally, without announcing each one, and at about 310 words it fills the two minutes at a natural speaking pace.
It has a clear narrative arc (the background, the course, the difficulty, the breakthrough, the reflection), which gives coherence without sounding scripted.
Precise, idiomatic vocabulary: 'keep myself afloat', 'deep-seated panic', 'something clicked', 'humbling, but also oddly liberating'.
Natural spoken markers ('What happened was', 'honestly', 'so to speak', 'by the way') and a range of past forms, including past perfect ('I'd never really learnt').
The final reflection answers 'explain why' with genuine insight, which lifts the talk beyond a simple story.

phrases: It was humbling but oddly liberating

questions: Is it harder to learn new skills as an adult than as a child?
How has the way adults learn new skills changed in recent years?
Should employers be responsible for training their workers?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of teaching yourself a skill online?
How do you think adult education will change in the future?

text: I think in some ways it is, but not for the reasons people usually give. There's a common idea that adults' brains are simply less flexible, and that may be true for certain things, like picking up a native-like accent in a foreign language. But I'd say the bigger obstacles are practical and psychological. Adults have far less free time, for one thing, and they're often much more afraid of looking foolish than children are. A child will happily fall off a bike twenty times; an adult tends to give up after the second attempt because it feels embarrassing. So adults might actually learn faster, if they could get past that.

Well, there's clearly a lot more demand for flexibility. Careers aren't as linear as they used to be, and someone might retrain two or three times in their working life, so learning has to fit around a job and a family. That's why online courses, part-time study and short professional qualifications have become so much more common. And I think the expectation has shifted, too. A generation ago, you finished your education and then simply worked; now employers increasingly expect people to keep updating their skills, and in some fields, like technology, what you learnt five years ago may already be out of date.

To some extent, yes. Employers benefit directly from a more skilled workforce, so it seems only reasonable for them to contribute, whether that's paying for courses or giving people time off to study. Many good companies already do this, partly because it helps them keep their staff. But I wouldn't want it to depend entirely on employers, because then the people in insecure or low-paid jobs, who arguably need retraining most, would be the least likely to get it. So I'd say it should be a shared responsibility, with the state making sure that nobody misses out simply because of who they happen to work for.

It's a mixed picture, I think. The obvious advantage is that the internet has made an enormous amount of knowledge freely available: you can learn to code, or bake bread, or play the guitar at two in the morning without paying a penny. On the other hand, the sheer volume of information can be overwhelming, and it's hard for a beginner to judge which sources are any good. There's also a lot to be said for the structure and feedback you get from a good teacher, someone who notices your mistakes before they turn into habits. Self-taught learners can end up with quite patchy knowledge.

I suspect the line between education and work will blur even further. Rather than front-loading education into the first twenty years of life, people will probably dip in and out of learning throughout their careers, taking a short course here and a qualification there whenever their work changes. Technology will make that easier, of course, and it wouldn't surprise me if employers started treating these smaller qualifications as seriously as degrees. Whether that's liberating or exhausting, though, will depend a lot on how well it's supported, because if people have to fund it all themselves, in their own time, it could become one more source of pressure.
notes: Each answer opens with a clear position and then develops it with reasons, examples or a qualification, which is the core of Part 3.
The speaker challenges assumptions ('not for the reasons people usually give') and weighs both sides, showing the flexibility of thought examiners reward at bands 8-9.
Abstract, precise vocabulary used naturally: 'linear careers', 'front-loading education', 'patchy knowledge', 'dip in and out of'.
Hedging is natural and varied: 'I'd say', 'arguably', 'to some extent', 'I suspect', 'It's a mixed picture'.
Complex structures (relative clauses, conditionals, cleft-style emphasis) appear without strain or error.
Each answer runs to roughly 100-115 words, about 40-45 seconds at a natural pace: long enough to develop a position with a reason, an example and a qualification, short enough to stay a conversation.

phrases: Not for the reasons people usually give
There's a lot to be said for…
